en: Commentary on the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Bodhisattvas, including the Most Victorious Son (Vasubandhu) and others.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
I pay homage to the Honored One, the Great Awakened One of gods and humans, whose merit and wisdom are both perfected;
to the sublime and wondrous True Dharma of unsurpassed words and meanings; and to the assembly of noble sages who correctly receive and study it.
I prostrate to the Unconquerable One of Great Compassion, who universally brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings;
having extensively gathered the essential meanings from the various sūtras, I shall briefly explain the Fivefold Yoga.
I take refuge in the wondrous power of concentration within the flow of Dharma, which gives rise to the name of unattached merit;
it is able to draw forth the supreme nectar of Dharma from the unsurpassed ocean of the Noble Ones.
Having partaken and received the sublime sound, they are spontaneously satisfied;
furthermore, for the benefit of all the worlds, an inexhaustible rain of flower-like syllables is poured down equally, nourishing and moistening the wish-fulfilling tree of the Muni.
This treatise is as preeminent as a lotus flower, Like a wondrous treasury of jewels within the great ocean;
It fully reveals the vast meaning of all vehicles, Skillfully explaining its text without omission.
Within this great treatise on yoga, I now provide a partial explanation according to my ability,
so that the True Dharma may remain forever inexhaustible and all sentient beings may receive benefit, peace, and happiness.
Now, for what purpose is this treatise expounded?
It is said that there are two reasons for expounding this treatise:
first, so that the unsurpassed Dharma-teaching of the Tathāgata may long abide in the world; [and second, so that sentient beings may easily understand it].
Second, for the sake of bringing about equal benefit and happiness for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are two reasons for expounding this treatise:

first, so that the sublime teaching of the Tathāgata’s nectar, which has already become obscured, may be recollected, collected, and once again revealed; [and second, so that those who have not yet entered the path may enter it, and those who have already entered it may progress toward the ultimate fruit].
As for "not being obscured," it is because questions, answers, and definitive resolutions flourish even more abundantly.

Second, within the realm of all sentient beings, those who possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) each cultivate supramundane goodness according to their own vehicle to attain the fruits of the three vehicles and emerge from birth and death;
those without the spiritual lineage cultivate mundane goodness according to the human or celestial vehicles to attain the fruits of humans and celestials and escape the miserable realms.
Furthermore, there are two reasons for expounding this treatise:

first, because some individuals, regarding various sūtras of provisional meaning that extensively teach emptiness, adhere to the literal expressions, thereby negating all existence and turning their backs on the teachings of existence; in order to lead them to realize that all phenomena possess characteristics, so that they may understand the sūtras' hidden intent and abandon the view of non-existence.

Second, there are those who, regarding many sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), adhere to the literal expressions and cling to the existence of all things, feeling aversion toward the teaching of emptiness; for their sake, so that they may realize the signlessness (*animitta*) of all phenomena, understand the hidden intent (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) of the sūtras, and abandon the view of existence, [the Buddha taught].
Furthermore, there are two reasons for expounding this treatise:
first, to bring to fulfillment those individuals (pudgala) who possess the bodhisattva lineage.

Relying solely upon the Great Teaching, they generate skillful wisdom regarding the texts, meanings, practices, and fruits of all vehicles; thereby severing all obstacles, cultivating all virtues, and realizing the Buddha’s Bodhi. Thus, until the end of the future, they never cease from bringing about the benefit and happiness of both themselves and others.
Second, for the sake of bringing to fruition those individuals belonging to the lineages of the two vehicles as well as those without a lineage:

they too rely upon the Great Teaching to generate skillful wisdom regarding the texts, meanings, practices, and fruits of their respective vehicles; thereby they sever the afflictive obscurations, suppress the various hindrances and entanglements, cultivate their own respective virtues, attain the fruits of their own vehicles, and achieve deliverance from the three realms and all evil destinies.
Furthermore, there are two reasons for expounding this treatise:

first, because some possess habitual ignorance, doubt, and perversion from past lives, and by adhering to the heterodox teachings of external paths and the provisional vehicles of the Lesser Vehicle, they are unable to believe in or understand the Mahāyāna; therefore, in order to skillfully distinguish the characteristics of the Mahāyāna dharma, so that they may develop faith and understanding, attain decisive realization, and depart from perversion.

Second, there are those who, upon hearing the various profound and difficult-to-understand intentions of the various sūtras, have their minds become confused and they slander them with disbelief; for the sake of benefiting them, one provides skillful exposition so that they may give rise to faith and understanding.
Furthermore, there are two reasons for expounding this treatise:
first, to benefit those who delight in concise discourse and are diligent in practice, by briefly analyzing the essential meanings of the Dharma collected from various sutras;
second, to benefit those who delight in extensive discourse and are diligent in preaching the Dharma, by revealing the boundless distinctions within each and every phenomenon.
Furthermore, there are two reasons for expounding this treatise:
first, to reveal the true nature of all phenomena by means of questions and answers that resolve and determine the establishment of the correct doctrine;
second, to eliminate all false attachments by means of questions and answers that refute erroneous doctrines.
Furthermore, there are two reasons for expounding this treatise:

first, to clarify that the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) exists conventionally but is non-existent in reality, while the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) exist in reality but are non-existent conventionally, thereby causing one to abandon the attachments of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*);

second, to clarify the distinctions between worldly reasoning and the gateways to the realization of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), thereby causing one to cultivate an unerring understanding of the two truths (*satyadvaya*).
Furthermore, there are two reasons for expounding this treatise:
first, to elucidate the two modes of reasoning—the conforming and the ultimate—so that one may understand that the teachings of the two pitakas and the three pitakas are not mutually contradictory;
second, to elucidate the four modes of reasoning—causality, representation-only, signlessness, and suchness—so that there may be distinctions in the cultivation of contemplative practice.
Furthermore, there are two reasons for expounding this treatise:
first, to manifest the distinctions among objects of experience, so that one may know the differences in the intrinsic nature, characteristics, and stages of all phenomena;
second, to manifest the distinctions among practices, so that one may know the differences between the expedient means, the roots, and the fruits of the three vehicles.
Regarding such categories of intended audiences, one should know that the various differing explanations found throughout the sūtras and śāstras all pertain to this treatise.
Now, what is the specific cause for the composition of this treatise?

It means that since beginningless time, all sentient beings have lacked knowledge regarding the true reality within the locus of all phenomena; through doubt, inversion, and perverse attachment, they give rise to various afflictions and initiate out-flowing karma, thereby cycling through the five destinies and undergoing the three great sufferings.

When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he employs skillful means as appropriate for each being to teach various sublime dharmas regarding the middle way and the true nature of reality, enabling all sentient beings to know that all phenomena are non-existent because they are empty in such and such a manner, and existent because they exist in such and such a manner. Thus, they thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena are neither empty nor existent, thereby distancing themselves from doubt, inversion, and biased attachment, and according to their respective spiritual lineages, they engage in the practice of the middle way, gradually cultivating it to fulfillment.
According to their respective capacities, they shall forever extinguish all hindrances, attain supreme enlightenment (*sambodhi*), and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, demonic activities will arise in profusion and sectarian attachments will compete for dominance, with many becoming attached to views of existence.

The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna realized the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) and, having collected the Mahāyāna teachings on signless emptiness, composed the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and other treatises to thoroughly elucidate the essential truth and eliminate the view of existence.
The noble Āryadeva and other great masters of treatises composed works such as the *Śataśāstra* to propagate and elucidate the Great Meaning.
Consequently, sentient beings again became attached to the view of emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*).

When the Bodhisattva Asaṅga attained the first bhūmi, he realized the Samādhi of Dharma-Light and acquired great supernormal powers. He served the Great Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya) and requested him to expound this treatise. It exhausts all principles, leaves no phenomena unexhausted, explains every word, elucidates every meaning, dispels all doubts, breaks all attachments, perfects all practices, and realizes all fruits. It is primarily for the sake of Bodhisattvas, so that they may attain skillfulness regarding the objects, practices, and fruits of all vehicles; it encourages them to diligently cultivate the great conduct and realize great enlightenment, and to constantly and unerringly teach sentient beings on a vast scale. Furthermore, it serves those of other vehicles, enabling them to rely on their own teachings to cultivate their respective practices and realize their respective fruits.
Thus has been briefly explained the basis for this treatise.
Now, regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, what are its name and meaning?

It is said that all dharmas—including the objects, practices, and fruits of all vehicles—are termed "yoga," because they all possess the sense of being associated with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

Regarding the yoga of objects: it refers to all objects being non-erroneous in nature, non-contradictory in nature, conducive in nature, and tending toward the ultimate; because they correspond with right reasoning, scripture, practice, and fruition, it is called yoga.

Although this yoga regarding objects applies universally to all things, various sūtras and śāstras present diverse explanations according to their specific characteristics and capacities. Some state that the four principles of phenomena—namely, dependence, function, nature, and proof—are called yoga, because they collectively encompass all correct principles.
Alternatively, it is said that among the twenty-four dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), one is named *yoga*, because cause and effect correspond to one another without contradiction.
Both of these [points] are explained extensively in various places, such as the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*.

Alternatively, it is said that the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) regarding both defilement and purification is called *yoga*, because it excels all others by eliminating what is discordant and conforming to what is harmonious, as stated in the *Mahābrahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra* and other scriptures.

All practitioners of yoga observe that there is not the slightest dharma that can be made to arise or made to cease, nor is there the slightest dharma they wish to realize or manifest through insight. That is to say, they practice within the yoga of the non-substantiality of all afflictions, observing that there is not the slightest dharma that can be made to arise or made to cease; and they practice within the yoga of the non-substantiality of all purities, observing that there is not the slightest dharma they wish to realize or manifest through insight.

Alternatively, it is said that ultimate, pure *tathatā* (suchness) is termed "yoga," because it is the most supreme within principle and is universally associated with all meritorious qualities, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

If one contemplates the ultimate reality, eliminating conceptual discrimination and remaining free from defilements, there will be neither a grasper nor anything grasped; there is neither liberation nor bondage. At that time, while in meditative concentration, one should perceive yoga and not harbor any doubts.
The *Mahārthasūtra* states that from one dharma up to a hundred dharmas, all are termed *yoga*, because although the dharma-gates differ, their meaning is not contradictory.

The *Vistarārthasūtra* states that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), truths (*satya*), and so forth, are all termed *yoga*, because they encompass all objects of cognition and accord with the capacities of sentient beings.
In such sūtras and śāstras as these, it is taught that all objects are termed *yoga* because they collectively possess the four natures and accord with the four dharmas.

As for "practicing *yoga*," this refers to all practices; because they accord with one another, conform to correct principle, follow the authentic teaching, and lead toward the true fruit, they are called *yoga*.

Although this practice of yoga (yogācāra) applies universally to all practices, various sūtras and śāstras provide diverse explanations according to their specific characteristics and the capacities of beings.

For instance, in the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exposition of the Yogācārabhūmi-sūtra), the term "yoga" refers to the correct cultivation of all practices, as it comprehensively subsumes all corresponding activities.

In the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*, the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) is termed "yoga," because this is the most excellent among all practices conducive to the result.
In the *Mahāṣaḍāyatanavibhaṅga-sūtra*, the balanced progression of śamatha and vipaśyanā is termed yoga, because such stillness observes all phenomena as primary.
In the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the cultivation of samādhi is termed "yoga," because it is the most powerful for stabilizing the mind and initiating practice.

In the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other texts, the four factors of faith, aspiration, skillful means (*upāya*), and diligence are termed "yoga," while attention (*manasikāra*) or wisdom (*jñāna*) is termed "skillful means" (*upāya*); these four give rise to all forms of practice.

In the *Śrutamayībhūmi*, the nine distinct paths are specifically identified and designated as "yoga" because they occupy superior positions within the stages of realizing the principles and eliminating delusions.

These consist of the mundane and supramundane paths of preparation (*prayoga*), uninterruptedness (*ānantarya*), liberation (*vimukti*), and advancement (*viśeṣa*), as well as the paths of the weak, medium, and superior grades. In the *Bhāvanāmayībhūmi*, the cultivation of all paths of remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*) is generally identified and designated as "yoga," for it provides a summary explanation for the benefit of those who prefer brevity.

In some places it is said that non-erroneous knowledge taking all stages (*bhūmi*) as its object is called yoga, because such non-erroneous knowledge regarding the phenomena of the stages is supreme among modes of practice.

In another place, it is further stated that either skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) or skillful means alone is termed *yoga*, because attention (*manasikāra*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) are superior in their initiation and execution, or because they are superior in their initial awakening.

In the *Sūtra on the True Nature of Merit*, it is stated that the contemplation of dependent origination is called yoga, because the wisdom of contemplating dependent origination is the most essential for escaping birth and death.
In the *Sūtra on Right Practice*, the Noble Eightfold Path—beginning with right view—is called "yoga," because it is the most excellent means for proceeding toward the city of Nirvāṇa.

In the *Vinaya Sūtra*, the cultivation of ethical discipline and so forth is termed "yoga," because these are the most excellent among the causes for the trainings in ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom.

In the *Mahārthasūtra*, it is stated that all distinctions in the stages of practicing mundane and supramundane deeds are termed "yoga," because they accord with and conform to the successive levels of correct practice.
Thus, all that is described as being practiced in common with the śrāvakas is termed *yoga*, because it is superior among the practices for realizing the three vehicles.
In the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the mental application (*manasikāra*) of contemplating emptiness is termed *yoga*, because it is the most excellent for initiating the great practice.

As that sutra says: "The great yoga of a bodhisattva is what is called the mental attention to emptiness; by means of this mental attention to emptiness, the bodhisattva does not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and is even able to purify all buddha-fields, and so forth."
In that same sutra, it further states that the name *prajñāpāramitā* is "superior yoga," because it guides the practice of the Mahāyāna in such an excellent manner. As that sutra says:

"Among all yogas possessed by bodhisattvas, the yoga of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the most supreme and most excellent... [as extensively explained] up to being 'unequaled with the unequaled.'"
Why is this? Because such a *prajñāpāramitā* is the unsurpassed yoga-dharma.

Elsewhere it is stated that the non-conceptual concentration (*avikalpa-samādhi*) subsumed within this perfection of wisdom is called "yoga," because it is capable of giving rise to all supreme qualities.

In another place, it is further stated that the simultaneous and equal operation of a bodhisattva’s extraordinary wisdom and compassion is called *yoga*, because it enables the realization of the great nirvana of non-abiding.

Such explanations as these, which describe various uncommon practices (*asādhāraṇa-caryā*), are termed *yoga*, because they are capable of realizing unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment (*anuttara-buddha-bodhi*).
Within such sūtras and śāstras, all practices are said to be named *yoga*, because they possess the four kinds of meanings described above.

Regarding "yoga of the fruit," it refers to all fruits; because they are mutually concordant, accord with correct reasoning, conform to the authentic teaching, and correspond to the true cause, they are designated as "yoga."

Although this fruition-yoga (*phala-yoga*) applies generally to all fruitions, various sūtras and śāstras provide diverse explanations according to their characteristics and capacities. Specifically, the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra* explains that the powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and unshared Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are called "yoga" because they can subdue all māras, refute all heterodox arguments, and triumph over other vehicles.
In the *Viśeṣacintibrahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, it is stated that the non-abiding nirvāṇa realized by the Buddha is called yoga, because it does not abide anywhere throughout the limits of the future.

In the *Mahārthasūtra*, it is stated that the non-conceptual wisdom and great compassion of the Tathāgata stage are called yoga, because they are eternally inexhaustible in benefiting both oneself and others.

In the *Vyākhyāyukti-yogācārabhūmi-sūtra*, all the merits of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) are termed *yoga*, because they extend to the limit of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) without interruption or exhaustion.
In the *Triyāna-guṇa-vibhaṅga-sūtra*, the meritorious virtues of the fruits of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are termed *yoga*, because they are all in accord with correct principle (*nyāya*).
The *Buddhapraśaṃsā-śāstra* states that the three bodies and the three virtues are all *yoga*, because all resultant qualities are inseparable from one another.

The *Saṃcayārtha-śāstra* states that the collection of all conditioned and unconditioned merits subsumed within the state of fruition is *yoga*, because it is the stage of ultimate integration through meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
In such sūtras and śāstras as these, all fruits and virtues are termed *yoga*, because they possess the aforementioned meanings.
Likewise, this sacred teaching is also termed *yoga*, because it accords with correct principle, conforms to correct practice, and leads to the attainment of the correct fruit.

There is an interpretation that the term *yoga* specifically refers to the contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*) of the three vehicles, because these involve repeated cultivation, accord with reason, proceed in accordance with the path, and result in the attainment of supreme fruits.
Furthermore, the object, the fruit, and the sacred teaching are also called *yoga*, because they are the objects of yoga, the fruits of yoga, and the treatises on yoga, respectively.

Thus, even these two characters of the word "yoga" in this treatise stir up the great ocean of the sublime teachings; how much more so would it be to explain the *Yogācārabhūmi* in its entirety? Fearing that it would be difficult to uphold, I have therefore provided but a brief exposition.

Practitioners of the three vehicles, by practicing such yoga through the successive stages of hearing, reflection, and so forth, fulfill it according to their respective capacities and gradually transform and guide all sentient beings; therefore, they are called yogācāras.

Alternatively, those Tathāgatas who have realized the perfection of yoga and, according to what is appropriate for each, maintain this yoga to discipline and transform all noble disciples, causing them to cultivate correct practice in successive stages, are called "yoga masters."

"Ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to the objective sphere, the basis, or the range of activity; alternatively, it has the sense of being "contained. It is called a ground because it is the objective sphere of practice for yogic practitioners, just as a "dragon-horse ground" is so named because one travels only upon it and does not go beyond.
Alternatively, because yogins increase the white dharmas (*śukladharma*) by relying on this locus, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*), like a field for sowing crops.
Alternatively, because the wisdom subsumed within the yogin’s ground manifests and increases in reliance upon this, it is called a "ground," like a ground of precious jewels.
Alternatively, because the yogācāra practices within this state and experiences the white dharmas (*śukladharma*), it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*), like the ground of a bull-king.

Alternatively, the Tathāgatas are called yogācāras; because they practice within the yoga of the non-conceptual realm (*aprapañca-dhātu*) and non-abiding nirvāṇa through their wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) and so forth, they are subsumed by it, and thus it is called a "ground."
Alternatively, there are seventeen levels (*bhūmi*), which encompass all practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*), just as one speaks of the "territory of a king.
Therefore, they are called the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Because it provides definitive analysis through question and answer regarding the essential nature and characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*), it is called a treatise (*śāstra*).
This treatise is titled as such because it is intended to enable the realization of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, just as the *Abhidharma-śāstra* is so named;
or alternatively, it is so designated because it unerringly explains the *Yogācārabhūmi*, just as the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* is so called.
Alternatively, this treatise is named after the stage upon which it relies, just as flowers are named for their habitat, such as "land" or "water" flowers.
For this reason, the title of the treatise is *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Now, the body of this treatise consists of five parts in total:
I. The *Maulī Bhūmi* (Basic Section) provides a concise and detailed analysis of the meaning of the seventeen stages (*bhūmi*).
II. The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Section on the Compendium of Determinations) concisely compiles and determines the profound and hidden essential meanings within those seventeen stages.
Third, the Section on the Compendium of Exegesis (*Vyākhyā-saṃgraha*), which briefly compiles the rules for explaining various sūtras.
Fourth, the Section on the Compendium of Synonyms (*Paryāya-saṃgraha*), which briefly compiles all the distinctions in the names and meanings of the phenomena found within the sūtras.
Fifth, the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī* briefly compiles the essential meanings of the various matters within the Three Piṭakas.
Since this treatise consists of these five parts, for what reason is it titled only the *Yogācārabhūmi*?
Regarding the initial establishment of the name, there is no error.
Furthermore, there is not a single dharma that is not a *yogācārabhūmi*, because the practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*) takes all dharmas as their objective conditions (*ālambana*).
In this context, I have been concise and have spoken of only seventeen [grounds].
Furthermore, these seventeen grounds comprehensively encompass all the textual and thematic content almost entirely.
As for the final four divisions, they serve to explain the essential textual and thematic points within the seventeen grounds; thus, they likewise do not depart from the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Therefore, this treatise takes the seventeen stages (*bhūmi*) as its essential core.

Although it comprehensively elucidates the objects and other factors of all vehicles, the intent of the author in posing questions and providing answers to determine the nature and characteristics of all phenomena is for the sake of bodhisattvas, so that they may attain skillfulness in everything, cultivate the fruit of buddhahood, and bring about inexhaustible benefit and happiness.
Therefore, this treatise belongs to the Abhidharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, for the purpose of enabling bodhisattvas to attain supreme knowledge.
The treatise asks:
What is the *yogācārabhūmi*?
This refers to the seventeen grounds.
The commentary states:
The initial question, "What is the *yogācārabhūmi*? asks generally about the essential core of this entire treatise.
The questioner previously heard the various sūtras speak of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, yet its meaning remained unclear; thus, he poses this question.

That is to say, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī on the Yogācārabhūmi Sūtra* frequently speaks of the correct cultivation of the *yogācārabhūmi*, and the *Candrapradīpa Sūtra* likewise speaks of practicing the *yogācārabhūmi*; such instances are not few, as explained extensively above.

Alternatively, the author of the treatise first accepted the general invitation; with the five parts of the body of the treatise fully present in his mind and wishing to provide a detailed explanation for his students, he provisionally raised a question as a means to initiate the discourse, thus asking: "What is the *Yogācārabhūmi*?"
If it were not so, there would have been no prior brief explanation, and there would have been no occasion for the sudden question, "What is this stage?
Furthermore, there are generally five types of those who pose questions:
first, questioning because of a lack of understanding; [and so forth].
2. Questioning out of doubt;
3. Questioning for the sake of testing;
4. Questioning out of contemptuous provocation.
Fifth, it is asked for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings.
This is the fifth [point], as this treatise is composed specifically for the purpose of benefiting and bringing happiness to all classes of sentient beings.
Regarding the "seventeen grounds," the *Yogācārabhūmi* that has been explained in its entirety consists briefly of seventeen grounds.
If established in detail, the stages (*bhūmi*) are boundless, because within each individual stage, the distinctions of its constituent phases (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) are themselves infinite.
Thus, this first turn consists of a general question and a general answer.
The treatise says:
What are the seventeen?
The summary verse (uddāna) states:
The mental consciousness associated with the five [sensory] consciousnesses, The three [types of mind] including those with vitarka and vicāra,
Those accompanied by samādhi and those that are neither, The states with mind and the state without mind,
Established through hearing, reflection, and cultivation— Thus are the three vehicles fully contained.
"With support and without support—these are called the seventeen stages.
The commentary asks:
For what reason is it asked again, "What are the seventeen?"?
Although they have heard the total number, they do not yet understand the individual names; therefore, they ask again.
As for *uḍḍāna*, it is first briefly answered in verse; because these collected names of the stages are bestowed upon students, it is called *uḍḍāna*.
"Associated with the five consciousnesses" refers to the stage associated with the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).
"Mind" refers to the mental stage (*manobhūmi*).
"The three, beginning with applied thought and sustained thought" refers to the three stages beginning with that which possesses both applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*).
"Accompanied by samādhi" refers to that which is accompanied by samādhi; this is called the stage of meditative equipoise (samāhita-bhūmi).
"Non-" refers to that which is not accompanied by samādhi; this is called the non-equipoised stage (a-samāhita-bhūmi).

This explanation is based on a single characteristic and merely distinguishes the names of the stages; it is not an exhaustive account of their principles, for these two names differ in their relative breadth and narrowness.
The term *samādhi* applies to both concentrated and non-concentrated states, occurring only when the mind is active (*sacittaka*);
the term *samāhita*, however, applies to both states with and without mind, yet is restricted exclusively to concentration, as will be explained in detail later.

Thus, those who possess the three vehicles do so by means of such stages as the stage of hearing, or by means of such higher stages; they thereby attain the three vehicles, as well as the stage with remainder and the stage without remainder.
The individual names for each are explained extensively below.
The treatise says:
First is the Stage Associated with the Five Collections of Consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya-saṃprayukta-bhūmi*).
Second, the stage of the mental faculty;
third, the stage with both vitarka and vicāra;
fourth, the stage with no vitarka and only vicāra.
Fifth, the stage without applied thought and sustained thought;
sixth, the stage of meditative equipoise;
seventh, the stage not of meditative equipoise.
Eighth is the stage with mind;
ninth is the stage without mind;
tenth is the stage consisting of what is heard.
Eleventh is the stage consisting of what is accomplished through reflection;
twelfth is the stage consisting of what is accomplished through cultivation;
thirteenth is the stage of the śrāvaka.
Fourteenth is the stage of the Pratyekabuddha;
fifteenth is the stage of the Bodhisattva;
sixteenth is the stage with remainder of support (*sopadhiśeṣabhūmi*).
Seventeenth is the stage of the nirvana without remainder.
Thus, these seventeen stages have been briefly explained; they are called the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
The commentary states:
Next, the names are listed in detail to provide a further response to the previous question.

Regarding the "Stage Associated with the Five Collections of Consciousness" (*pañcavijñānakāyasaṃprayuktā bhūmi*), this refers to the sense faculties such as the eye, which serve as the specific, non-common supports for the visual consciousness and so forth; for the eye and other faculties do not serve as supports for any other types of consciousness.
Furthermore, they are immediate supports, because the sharpness or dullness of the consciousnesses corresponds to the keenness or bluntness of the eyes and other faculties.
Moreover, they are simultaneous supports, as they must exist together, unlike the mind (*manas*) and its objects.

For these reasons, the five consciousnesses are designated by names derived from their respective sense organs—just as one speaks of "barley sprouts" or "the sound of a drum"—and are thus called the "five consciousnesses."

Because its supporting faculty (indriya) possesses physical resistance (sapratigha), and because it is necessarily not separate from the body that serves as its support—just like bodily sensation (kāyikavedanā)—it is called "body" (kāya).

Furthermore, "body" (kāya) carries the sense of "basis" (āśraya) and the sense of "substance" (dravya), as in the "group of six consciousnesses" (ṣadvijñānakāya) or the "group of six volitions" (ṣaṭcetanākāya); since this stage is established based upon the group of five consciousnesses, it is therefore termed "associated" (saṃprayukta).
As stated in the Vinaya, there are discourses concerning kings (*rāja-saṃyukta*) and discourses concerning thieves (*caura-saṃyukta*), meaning discussions that arise based on kings and thieves.
This is also the case here: although many phenomena are analyzed within this stage, the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are predominant; therefore, they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, the mental states associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness are collectively termed "associated.
Although many factors are clarified within this stage, they are explained separately because the mind and its mental concomitants are predominant.
Furthermore, "concomitance" (saṃprayoga) has the meaning of being subsumed under or belonging to.

This refers to the factors subsumed under the five groups of consciousness (pañca-vijñāna-kāya) as taught in this stage; because these consist of their own nature, their support, their object, their associates, and their activity, they are called "concomitant."
The grounds are as previously explained.

From this point onward, the various grounds associated with the groups of consciousness (vijñānakāya) also possess commonalities as appropriate to each case; however, they are not mentioned here for the sake of brevity.
As for what is called the "mental ground" (manobhūmi), it refers to the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses, which all rely upon the mental faculty (manas-indriya).
By omitting the three terms associated with the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-kāya*), one speaks only of "mind" (*manas*).

Furthermore, although there are eight consciousnesses from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there are only six consciousnesses from the perspective of conventional capacity (*yathā-vṛtti*).
The sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses are all subsumed under the sixth; they are referred to simply as "mind" (*manas*) because they are designated by the name of their support (*āśraya*).
Since their support is non-material (*arūpa*), or because it is distinct from the body—just as the mind and feelings are—it is not called the "body."
The corresponding [explanations] follow the previous pattern and are thus omitted here.

Furthermore, although the sixth, seventh, and eighth [consciousnesses] all equally possess the meaning of *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*—since they are subsumed under the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), the sense-base of mind (*mana-āyatana*), and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) respectively—they are referred to simply as "mind" (*manas*) because their specific meanings are distinct, and they are all subsumed under the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) which functions as deliberation (*santīraṇa*).
The eighth [consciousness] is predominant in the sense of "mind" (*citta*) as the holder of seeds;

the sixth is predominant in the sense of "cognition" (*vijñāna*) as the universal discernment of objects. For this reason, they are not designated as the "ground of mind" (*cittabhūmi*) or the "ground of cognition" (*vijñānabhūmi*).
The body and its associated factors are not mentioned here because they are treated briefly.
The meaning of "level" (*bhūmi*) is as explained previously.
For what reason are the five consciousnesses combined into a single level and taught first, while the remaining consciousnesses are established as a single level and taught second?

Since the five consciousnesses are likewise non-existent [in that state], their functions—such as the differentiation of objects—will be explained; however, because the matters discussed are few, they are combined and established as one, and are mentioned first.
The mental ground (manobhūmi) is the reverse of this, and thus it is established separately as one, and is mentioned second.

Furthermore, because the five consciousnesses rely on the same material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) and take the same material objects (*rūpaviṣaya*) as their conditions, they are established together as one.
Because the remaining [consciousness] relies on non-material [bases] and its objects are indeterminate, it is established separately as one.
Because their intrinsic natures, bases, objects, and degrees of coarseness or subtlety follow a sequential order, they are described as preceding and succeeding one another.
Furthermore, because the five consciousnesses are equally subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they are established together as a single category and said to occur at the very beginning.

The remaining consciousnesses are indeterminate; they are subsumed under either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Therefore, one is established separately and said to reside in the second [category].

Thus, these two stages—by combining their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), objective support (*ālambana*), retinue (*parivāra*), and activity (*karma*) as their essence—subsume all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).

It should be understood that herein, because all phenomena are not separate from consciousness, because they arise based on consciousness, because consciousness is their essence, and because consciousness is preeminent, the two stages are first established in reliance upon the eight consciousnesses.
These eight consciousnesses—their intrinsic nature, bases, objects, associates, and functions—will be explained in detail later.
Regarding the three stages that possess vitarka and vicāra: *vitarka* refers to seeking.
Vicāra refers to investigation.
It is either volition (cetanā) or wisdom (prajñā) that seeks out an object; its coarse state is called vitarka.
When these two examine the object with subtlety, their subtle state is called vicāra.
Two dharmas do not correspond within a single moment, because their respective categories of grossness and subtlety differ across preceding and succeeding phases.
Based on these two [factors], the three stages are established. There is an interpretation which states:

These three are established based on the correspondence between the two preceding and succeeding stages; that is, the level of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna are called the stage with vitarka and vicāra (*savitarkasavicārabhūmi*), because the coarse mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) therein can exist in a continuous succession where vitarka and vicāra are associated together.

In the intermediate dhyāna, there is a continuous succession of coarse mind and mental factors; since there is definitely no *vitarka* (applied thought) and it can only be associated with *vicāra* (sustained thought), it is called the stage of "without *vitarka* and with *vicāra* only."

In all stages from the second dhyāna upward, the continuous succession of mind and mental factors is invariably dissociated from vitarka and vicāra; this is termed the stage without vitarka and without vicāra.

If the levels of the desire realm and the first dhyāna, as well as the subtle mind and mental factors of the intermediate dhyāna that are not associated with vitarka and vicāra, along with all material phenomena, all non-associated formations, and all unconditioned phenomena—because they are not associated with vitarka and vicāra—are also said to be the "levels without vitarka and without vicāra."
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "The stage with vitarka and vicāra, and the stage without vitarka and with only vicāra, are exclusively stages possessing mind.

The mindless sleep, the mindless fainting, the attainment of non-ideation, birth in the realm of non-ideation, the attainment of cessation, and the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder are called the stages without mind."
There is an interpretation:

these three are established based on the stages of detachment from desire. Specifically, regarding the phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna that are conventionally designated as persons, if they have not yet become detached from both *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought), it is called the stage with *vitarka* and *vicāra*.

Regarding the provisional designations for the phenomena of the intermediate dhyāna: when one has already abandoned desire for *vitarka* (applied thought) but has not yet abandoned desire for *vicāra* (sustained thought), it is called the stage of "without *vitarka*, with only *vicāra*.

Regarding the provisional designations for the phenomena of the stages from the second dhyāna upward: when one has abandoned both *vitarka* and *vicāra*, it is called the stage of "without *vitarka* and without *vicāra*."
If one has already become detached from desire while on a lower stage, that stage may also be described as "without vitarka and vicāra.

Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "In this context, it is called the stage without vitarka and vicāra because of the detachment from the desire for vitarka and vicāra, not because they do not manifest."

Why is this so? Because even for one who has not yet abandoned the desires of the desire realm, through the specific application of mental attention (*manasikāra*) based on instruction, there may also at times arise the activity of a mind that is without applied thought (*vitarka*) and without sustained thought (*vicāra*).

"One who has already abandoned applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) may still have applied and sustained thought manifesting, as when emerging from that meditative absorption or being born in that stage.

According to the true meaning, these three are established solely in terms of realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*): namely, because both applied and sustained thought are obtainable therein among the contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna, it is called the "first stage."
The contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas within the intermediate dhyāna are called the second stage because therein there is no vitarka (applied thought) and only vicāra (sustained thought).
The contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas in all stages above the second dhyāna are called the third stage because therein both vitarka and vicāra are entirely absent.

Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "In this context, the desire realm and the first dhyāna—whether in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) or as a birth (*upapatti*)—are called the stage with vitarka and vicāra.
The intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), whether in meditative absorption or as a birth, is called the stage without vitarka and with only vicāra."

From the second dhyāna upward, including the entirety of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), are designated as the stage of being without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*).
Furthermore, the uncontaminated conditioned first dhyāna concentration is also designated as the stage of having applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarkasavicārā bhūmiḥ*).

"Because one enters this meditative absorption by relying on the dharmas that serve as the basis for vitarka and vicāra, taking *tathatā* (suchness) as the object, and because no conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) manifests therein;
the rest is as previously explained."
If the three stages were established based on association (*samprayoga*) and detachment from desire (*vairāgya*), they would fail to encompass all phenomena and would result in great confusion.
Although it is said that stages such as "with vitarka and vicāra" consist solely of mind, this is a coarse delineation of the characteristics of the stages from a single perspective.

Within this context, it is taught that among the stages from the second dhyāna upward where there is neither vitarka nor vicāra, the state of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the birth of non-conceptual beings (asaṃjñi-sattva-upapatti), and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are called the "mindless ground" (acittaka-bhūmi); all other states are called the "ground with mind" (sacittaka-bhūmi).
Thereafter follow four gates, which are established differently as will be explained later.

Although it is said here that a stage is called "without applied thought and sustained thought" because of being free from the desire for applied and sustained thought, this only refers to the stages from the second dhyāna upward, which are necessarily free from the desire for the stages involving applied and sustained thought. It does not mean that those factors of lower stages which are already free from the desire for applied and sustained thought may also be called "without applied thought and sustained thought."

If this were the case, then even those who have not yet abandoned the vitarka and vicāra of the lower stages would have to be said to possess vitarka and vicāra with respect to the dharmas of the higher stages.
To establish it in such a manner would result in great confusion.
Therefore, these three are established solely in terms of the upper and lower realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*).
As for what is called the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*), it refers to the stage of superior concentration.

Because it is free from dullness and agitation, it can equally induce [the mind], or it induces equanimity, or it is that which is induced by equanimity; thus, it is named the stage of "evenly induced" (*samāhita*).
One interpretation holds that this name applies exclusively to all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) accompanied by mind, because these alone are capable of equally inducing meritorious qualities.
It does not extend to mindless states, as the preceding verse specifies that they are "conjoined with *samādhi*."

Samādhi is a mental factor (caitta) among the factors with specific objects; therefore, because the two mindless attainments cannot evenly induce all meritorious qualities, they are not stages of equipoise (asamāhita-bhūmi).
If that is so, why is it explained in terms of the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*)?
Briefly stated, there are four types of this stage of meditative equipoise: namely, the dhyānas, the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the concentrations (*samādhi*), and the attainments (*samāpatti*).
"Dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas.
"Vimokṣa" refers to the eight liberations.
"Samādhi" refers to the emptiness samādhi, the wishlessness samādhi, and the signlessness samādhi.

Regarding "attainments" (samāpatti), they refer to the five attainments of direct perception, the eight attainments of the bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), the ten attainments of the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana), the four attainments of the formless (ārūpya), the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
There is no fault here.
These two mindless attainments are called "equipoise" because they are the fruit of equipoise, though in reality they are not equipoise. According to another interpretation:

This name applies to both states with mind and states without mind. Regarding the essential nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), if it is a state with mind, it is called "even-conduct" (*samāhita*) because it can equally induce all meritorious qualities, because it also induces the equilibrium of the faculties, the primary elements, and so forth, and because it is induced by even means such as the absence of laxity and excitement, and the lack of remorse due to ethical discipline. Thus, it is named "even-conduct."

If there were no meditative absorption of the mindless state, although it could not induce superior qualities, it would nevertheless induce the faculties, the primary elements, and so forth, which are equal; because it is induced by this state of equanimity, it is also called "equipoise" (samāhita).
If that is so, why does the preceding verse state that it is "concomitant with samādhi"?
There is no fault here.

The verse is concise and merely says they are concomitant; in reality, meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) is not concomitant [with the mind], because equipoise was also subsequently stated to pervade even the mindless states.

Regarding the meaning as it truly is: the term "stage of meditative equipoise" (*samāhita-bhūmi*) has both a general and a specific sense. It is called "general" because it encompasses both states of mind and mindlessness;

this is because the subsequent mention of the non-conceptual attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) also constitutes the essence of the stage of meditative equipoise.
It exists only in impure and pure superior meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), and not in all distracted states of mind such as those of the desire realm; therefore, it is called "restricted.

This is because the subsequent statement specifies that only the dhyānas and so forth are termed the "ground of meditative equipoise" (*samāhita-bhūmi*), and that one-pointedness of mind in the desire realm is not produced by such equipoise.
It is induced by freedom from regret, joy, and bliss; the desire realm is not so.
By this same principle, in the higher realms, if one is in a state of distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), it is likewise not meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), for it is the same as the desire realm.
Based on this relative distinction, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be established.

First, there are states that are associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) but do not belong to the non-concentrated stage (*asamāhita-bhūmi*), namely, the mind and mental factors associated with *samādhi* during moments of distracted mind within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth.
Or, there are states of meditative equipoise that are not accompanied by concentration (*samādhi*);

namely, the essence of *samādhi* during the state of equipoise, as well as all phenomena existing in the states of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Alternatively, there are those that are both associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and belong to the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*), namely: all the dhyānas, the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and the minds and mental factors within the states of conscious meditative absorption, excluding the factor of concentration itself (*samādhi*).
Or there may be cases where neither applies, namely, excluding all dharmas belonging to the higher stages.
Furthermore, the terms *samādhi*, *samāpatti*, and *samāhita* differ in their breadth and scope.

The term "samādhi" refers to the mental factor (caitta) of one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā), which subsumes all instances of one-pointedness of mind within any state accompanied by consciousness, encompassing both concentrated and non-concentrated states.
However, while various sūtras and śāstras refer to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), and so forth as "samādhi" only in their predominant sense,
*samāpatti* generally designates the essential nature of concentration within all states— whether with or without mind— that constitute meditative equipoise.

In various sūtras and śāstras, those meditative concentrations that correspond to the five types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth are specifically designated as "attainments" (*samāpatti*).

The term "equipoise" (*samāhita-bhūmi*), however, refers generally to all qualities of the states of both mind-with-mind and mind-without-mind; therefore, within this stage, it universally encompasses all qualities of the meditative states.
Because it is comprehensive in this way, the name of the stage is applied specifically to it.

As for the statement that it is not the *asamāhita-bhūmi* (the non-concentrated stage), the opposite of the preceding [definition] is easily understood, so there is no need for an extensive explanation.
These two stages collectively encompass all dharmas belonging to both the concentrated (*samāhita*) and non-concentrated states.
Regarding the statement that there are stages with mind and stages without mind, the distinctions are briefly established by way of five gates.

First, the gate of general exposition according to the stages (*bhūmi*): namely, the stage associated with the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), the stage with vitarka and vicāra, and the stage without vitarka and with only vicāra. These four are invariably stages with mind.

Within the stage devoid of both vitarka and vicāra, with the exception of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the birth-state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), all remaining states are exclusively stages possessing mind (*sacittaka*).

If the attainment of non-conception, the birth-state of non-conception, and the attainment of cessation are considered stages devoid of mind (*acittaka*), then within this framework, even sleep without mind and fainting without mind are termed "possessing mind" because they still involve seven or eight mental factors; thus, only the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) such as the attainment of non-conception and others, which are contrary to mind, are designated as stages devoid of mind.
Second, the gate of the mind being distracted or undistracted refers to the four inversions and so forth.
A mind that is inverted and distracted is called the "mindless ground" (*acittabhūmi*), because it has lost its original nature.
Third, the gate of the mind arising or not arising refers to the fact that if the conditions are complete, this mind can arise; this is called the "ground with mind" (*sacittabhūmi*).
If that mind does not arise because its conditions are incomplete, it is called the "mindless stage" (*acittabhūmi*).
Within this framework, when such a mind arises, it is called the "mindful stage" (*sacittabhūmi*); when that mind does not arise, it is called the "mindless stage."
4. The Gate of Establishing by Way of States: This refers to excluding six states, which are termed the "state with mind" (*sacittikā bhūmi*).

If one is in the state of sleep without mind, the state of fainting without mind, the state of the non-conceptual attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the state of birth in the non-conceptual realm (*asaṃjñika*), the state of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or the state of the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*), these are termed the "state without mind" (*acittikā bhūmi*).

Fifth, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), it is said that only within the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) do all minds cease, which is termed the "mindless stage" (*acittabhūmi*). In other states, one is conventionally designated as "mindless" because the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are absent; however, because the eighth consciousness has not yet been extinguished, it is termed the "stage with mind" (*sacittabhūmi*).
Thus, these two stages have various distinctions in their gates, with progress and regression being indeterminate.

Regarding the stage consisting of what is heard (*śrutamaya-bhūmi*): it refers to the wisdom arising from hearing that understands the meaning of the texts, as well as the mind and mental factors associated with that wisdom.

The stage consisting of that which is accomplished through reflection (*cintāmayī bhūmi*) refers to the wisdom arising from the understanding of the characteristics of phenomena produced by reflection, as well as the mental states and mental factors associated with that wisdom.

The stage consisting of that which is accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī bhūmi*) refers to the wisdom arising from the understanding of both principles and phenomena produced by cultivation, as well as the mental states and mental factors associated with that wisdom.
"Listening" (śruta) refers to hearing; that is, when the ear-faculty gives rise to the auditory consciousness, one hears the verbal teachings.
"Reflection" (cintā) refers to deliberation; that is, the mental factor of volition (cetanā), which gives rise to wisdom by means of discerning and investigating phenomena (dharma).

"Cultivation" (bhāvanā) refers to the practice of cultivation, which is precisely the superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that gives rise to wisdom by cultivating the remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
From these three types [of concentration], the three kinds of wisdom (*prajñā*) and their associated mental factors arise; these are collectively termed the essence of the three stages.
The broad meaning of the three types of wisdom will be analyzed later.
Thus, these three stages have as their intrinsic nature the mental states and mental factors belonging to the categories of the three types of wisdom, along with the fruits attained thereby.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "The stage consisting of cultivation is also both the stage with remainder and the stage without remainder.
As for the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, it refers to the Buddha’s holy teaching, wherein sound is the primary medium.
Having heard this teaching from teachers and friends, they cultivate and realize it through successive stages, thereby forever transcending the world.
Because their practice is minor and their fruit is minor, they are called *śrāvakas* (Hearers).
Thus, the spiritual lineage of such *śrāvakas*, including their initial resolve, cultivation, and attainment of the fruit, is collectively termed the "Stage of the Śrāvaka."

As for the stage of the Pratyekabuddha: they always delight in tranquility and do not desire to dwell among the crowd; having perfected their preparatory practices, they attain spontaneous and solitary awakening without the instruction of teachers or friends, forever transcending the world.
Because they attain the middling fruit through middling practice, they are called *pratyekabuddhas*.
Alternatively, because they awaken to the noble fruit by depending upon conditions, they are also called *pratyayabuddhas*.
Thus, the lineage of the *pratyekabuddha*, including the generation of the mind, the practice, and the attainment of the fruit—all these taken together are termed the *pratyekabuddhabhūmi*.

The Bodhisattva-bhūmi refers to those who seek great enlightenment out of compassion for sentient beings; or those whose aspiration for bodhi is firm and fierce, who practice and realize it over a long period of time, and who forever transcend the mundane world.
Because they possess great practice and great fruit, they are called Bodhisattvas.
Thus, the lineage of a Bodhisattva, the arousal of the mind, the cultivation of practice, and the attainment of the fruit—all these taken together are collectively termed the "Bodhisattva-bhūmi."
The great meaning of the three vehicles shall be extensively analyzed later.
Regarding the stage of "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*), this refers to the stage of nirvāṇa with remainder.
"Remainder" (*upadhi*) refers specifically to the basis of outflows (*āsrava*); briefly, there are eight kinds.

First, the basis of designation (*prajñapti-adhiṣṭhāna*), namely the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*); because one relies upon these, the conventional designations of a person, such as "caste" (*jāti*) and so forth, are established.

Second, the basis of appropriation (*parigraha-adhiṣṭhāna*), namely the seven objects of appropriation (*sapta-parigraha-vastu*), which are: one's own father and mother, wife and children, slaves, servants, laborers, friends, and kinsmen.
Third, the basis of maintenance (*sthiti-adhiṣṭhāna*), which refers to the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*).

Fourth, the basis of transmigration (*pravṛtti-adhiṣṭhāna*), which refers to the four stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*) and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Fifth, the basis of obstruction (*āvaraṇa-adhiṣṭhāna*), which refers to all devas and māras.
Sixth, the basis of suffering and affliction, which refers to the various realms of the desire world (*kāmadhātu*).
Seventh, the basis of satisfaction, which refers to the bliss of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Eighth, the basis of the final limit, which refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) within the continuum of an Arhat.
Now, taking the entirety of the final basis and excluding the six bases of conciliation (*saṃgrahavastu*), one takes the remaining portion which constitutes the obstacle to transmigration.
Furthermore, within this stage there are four kinds of tranquility (*śānti*):
first, the tranquility of suffering, which means that future suffering will never again arise.
Second is the tranquility of afflictions, meaning that all defilements ultimately do not arise.
Third is the tranquility of action, meaning not committing evil and cultivating various virtues.

Fourth is the tranquility of equanimity, meaning the six constant abidings: remaining neither joyful nor sorrowful at the gates of the six sense faculties, dwelling in sublime equanimity with right mindfulness and right situational awareness.

Arhats and others who abide in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*) possess the four types of tranquility and have a small remainder of dependence; therefore, it is called the stage with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*).

This stage consists of all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas within the bodies of those in the no-more-learning stage of the two vehicles, taken collectively as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Although the Tathāgata lacks a truly real body and mind as well as the remaining support of outflows (*āsrava-śeṣa-niśraya*), he possesses transformational manifestations that resemble such a support of outflows; therefore, even from the perspective of these manifested characteristics, it can be said that he abides in the stage of "having a remaining support" (*sa-upadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*).
The stage of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*) refers to the stage of nirvāṇa with no remainder.
All remaining bases of outflows (*sāsrava-upadhi*) are relinquished, and even the conditioned, untainted (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) states of the two vehicles are relinquished.
Although the Tathāgata possesses conditioned, untainted [qualities], he is devoid of all tainted residual supports; therefore, this stage is also called the "ground of no-residual support.

Within this ground, there exist only the profound merits manifested by pure *tathatā*, which are free from all conceptual discrimination and severed from all frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*); they cannot be described as aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), or as humans, devas, and so forth.
Whether identical or distinct, whether existent or non-existent, all names and characteristics are merely provisional designations. According to one interpretation:

the nature of this stage consists primarily of the ultimate unconditioned *tathatā* (suchness) as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), while also incorporating the conditioned, untainted merits of the Tathāgata.

Because the Tathāgata’s merit is profoundly deep, devoid of marks, and ineffable, it is not explicitly stated that it also encompasses the five consciousnesses, the stages (*bhūmi*), and so forth; yet in principle, it indeed does encompass them.
One interpretation holds:

the Tathāgata’s conditioned merits are subsumed under the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder), while his unconditioned merits are subsumed under the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).

Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "In the stage of no-remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa), there is one part of five stages, namely: the stage of no-mind (acittikā bhūmiḥ), the stage produced by cultivation (bhāvanāmayī bhūmiḥ), and the stages of the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva."
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā, Volume One.
